overview: Cayton Bay is a cliff-backed bay roughly four miles south of Scarborough, one of the string of sandy bays along this stretch of coast between Scarborough and Filey. The council describes it as a small sandy bay backed by cliffs, with a mix of sand and rock, and it's a long-standing favourite with surfers and with visitors from the holiday park above.

The cliffs here are on the move. A major landslip in April 2008 near Osgodby left bungalows on the Knipe Point estate at the cliff edge, and the slope and the National Trust land below it are a Site of Special Scientific Interest. Look out too for the Second World War pillboxes, many of them damaged by coastal erosion.

The National Park describes Cayton as a place for more powerful breaks for experienced surfers, especially in winter and spring, and as one of the few spots around here that can be surfed at both low and high tide. A surf school and shop operate from the clifftop car park all year. Beginners are best off booking a lesson rather than going it alone.

text: Cayton has several distinct breaks rather than one. Surf-forecast lists a sandbar break at the Bunkers, which it says is best around high tide, and a separate point break, both working best on a north swell; it gives south-westerly winds as best at the Bunkers and westerly at the Point. That variety is why the National Park says the bay can be surfed at low and high tide.

This is where Scarborough's surfers come when they want more push. Surf-forecast warns about rocks, rips and pollution, and expects crowds at the Bunkers when there's swell, while the Point is usually quieter. If you're still learning, book a lesson rather than paddling out alone.

Think of Cayton as three separate waves. The Pumphouse is a rocky patch that throws up quick, hollow lefts and tends to be best from low to mid tide. The Bunkers, in front of the old wartime concrete, is a sandbar that holds up through high tide and is the intermediate's pick. The Point is the exposed end, a left that peels on a north swell with a westerly wind; it's for experienced surfers only, with rocks, rips and the odd bit of pollution to think about.

The catch is the walk: it's a steep climb back up from the beach, so pack light. It's usually less busy than Scarborough, and when it's working you'll see locals spread across all three spots. Learners should head to Scarborough's South Bay or book a lesson instead of picking a peak here.

cards.label: Conditions
cards.title: North swell, westerly winds
cards.text: Surf-forecast rates north swell best; SW wind at the Bunkers, W at the Point.

cards.title: Rocks and rips

practical.label: Lifeguards
practical.title: RNLI, 10am–6pm
practical.text: In 2026 RNLI lifeguards patrolled from 2 May, at weekends through early May and then daily until 6 September.

practical.label: Parking
practical.title: Clifftop car park
practical.text: Cayton Bay beach car park is at Killerby Cliff (YO11 3NR). It's a grass field that can be tricky after heavy rain.

practical.label: Access
practical.title: Steep path down
practical.text: The path from the car park to the beach is steep and not suitable for wheelchairs or people with poor balance.

practical.label: Facilities
practical.title: By the car park
practical.text: Toilets and a surf shop sit next to the clifftop car park; the council also lists a café and shop.

practical.label: Dogs
practical.title: Allowed
practical.text: The council lists dogs as allowed, and Cayton isn't one of the zones in the Scarborough-area seasonal beach ban.

practical.label: Parking
practical.title: Pay car park by the old surf shop
practical.text: There is a pay car park at the top by the former surf shop, with changing rooms and showers. Roadside parking nearby is restricted, so use the car park.

faqs.q: Is Cayton Bay good for beginners?
faqs.a: Only with an instructor. The National Park describes Cayton's breaks as more powerful and aimed at experienced surfers; Scarborough's bays are gentler for learning on your own.

faqs.q: What tide is best at Cayton Bay?
faqs.a: It depends on the break. The National Park says Cayton can be surfed at both low and high tide, and surf-forecast rates the Bunkers best around high tide.

faqs.q: Can you take dogs to Cayton Bay?
faqs.a: Yes. The council lists dogs as allowed, and the bay isn't covered by the summer beach bans in the Scarborough-area dog control order.
Not easily. The path down from the clifftop car park is steep and unsuitable for wheelchairs.

faqs.q: Which part of Cayton Bay is best?
faqs.a: The Bunkers suit most improvers because the sandbar holds through the tide. The Pumphouse is quicker and hollower, and the Point is for experienced surfers only.
